right.question: How is a critical fatigue area defined for aircraft control cables?
right.answer: A critical fatigue area is defined as the working length of a cable where the cable runs over, under, or around a pulley, sleeve, or through a fair-lead; any section where the cable is flexed, rubbed, or worked in any manner; or any point within 1 foot of a swaged-on fitting [1].

right.question: How do I find broken wires in a control cable during an inspection?
right.answer: To find broken wires in a control cable during an inspection, pass a cloth over the critical fatigue areas to snag on broken wires, which will clean the cable for a visual inspection and detect broken wires if the cloth snags on the cable. Additionally, perform a very careful visual inspection since a broken wire may not protrude but may lie in the strand and remain in the helix position, potentially showing up as a hairline crack; if a broken wire of this type is suspected, further inspection with a magnifying glass of 7 power or greater is recommended [2].

right.question: When must a kinked control cable or one with a popped core be replaced?
right.answer: A kinked control cable or one with a popped core must be replaced regardless of wear or broken wires. [2]

right.question: How much can the outer wires of a control cable wear before the cable has to be replaced?
right.answer: The outer wires of a control cable must be replaced when they appear to blend together, which occurs when the outer wires are worn 40 to 50 percent. [1]

right.question: What proof load is used to test cable terminals and splices before installation?
right.answer: 60 percent of the cable breaking strengths given in Table 7-3 and Table 7-4 [1].

right.question: What is the minimum edge distance and spacing for a single row of rivets?
right.answer: For a single row of rivets, the edge distance should not be less than 2 times the diameter of the rivet and the spacing should not be less than 3 times the diameter of the rivet. [1]

right.question: What slope is the steepest allowed for a scarf patch in a plywood skin?
right.answer: The steepest slope permitted for all kinds of plywood in a scarf patch is 1 in 12 [1].

right.question: What diameter of safety wire should I use with the double-twist method on parts with large holes?
right.answer: .032-inch diameter safety wire should be used with the double-twist method on parts that have a hole diameter larger than .045 inch [1].

right.question: After safetying a turnbuckle, how many threads of the terminal may still show?
right.answer: No more than three threads of the turnbuckle threaded terminal should be exposed [1].

right.question: What resistance must the electrical bond between a piece of equipment and the aircraft structure have?
right.answer: Less than 2.5 milliohms [1].

right.question: What is galvanic corrosion and how can I recognise it?
right.answer: Galvanic corrosion occurs when two dissimilar metals make contact in the presence of an electrolyte. It is usually recognizable by the presence of a buildup of corrosion at the joint between the metals [1].

right.question: What does exfoliation corrosion look like and where does it usually show up?
right.answer: Exfoliation corrosion shows itself by lifting up the surface grains of a metal by the force of expanding corrosion products occurring at the grain boundaries just below the surface [1]. It usually shows up on extruded sections where grain thickness is usually less than in rolled forms [1].

right.question: Why does heated titanium change colour, and should the coloured film be removed?
right.answer: Heated titanium changes colour because different oxides form on its surface at various temperature ranges: a blue oxide at 700–800 °F, a purple oxide at 800–950 °F, and a gray or black oxide at 1,000 °F or higher [1]. These coatings are protective discolorations and should not be removed [1].

right.question: Which torque values do I use for nuts and bolts when the manufacturer gives none?

right.question: What goes wrong if a vented fuel tank cap is replaced with an unvented one?
right.answer: Fuel starvation and possible collapse of the fuel tank or cell occurs. [1]

right.question: Can a metal fuel tank be welded or soldered, and what has to be done first?
right.answer: Yes, a metal fuel tank can be welded or soldered, but only if it has been adequately purged of fuel fumes [2]. First, the tank must be purged of fuel fumes [2].

right.question: How far apart can clamps be when supporting wires and cables in an aircraft?
right.answer: Clamps should be installed at intervals of not more than 24 inches when supporting wires and cables, except when the wires are contained in troughs, ducts, or conduits. [1]

right.question: Which gas is recommended for inflating aircraft tires, and which must never be used?
right.answer: Nitrogen is recommended for inflating aircraft tires, and oxygen must never be used. [1]

right.question: Why is it dangerous to service lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries in the same area?
right.answer: It is dangerous to service lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries in the same area because introduction of acid electrolytes into alkaline electrolyte will destroy the nickel-cadmium battery and vice-versa [1].

right.question: Which materials can be checked with magnetic particle inspection?

right.question: How reliable is a mechanical punch tester for judging the condition of aircraft fabric?
right.answer: A mechanical punch tester is not reliable for judging the condition of aircraft fabric because its accuracy depends on individual device calibration, total coating thickness, brittleness, and types of coatings and fabric. It is especially inaccurate for glass fiber fabric, which will easily shear and indicate a very low reading regardless of the true breaking strength. Additionally, if the fabric tests in the lower breaking strength range with the mechanical punch tester or if the overall fabric cover conditions are poor, more accurate field tests may be required [1].

right.question: How should oxygen and fuel gas cylinders be secured in a welding area?

right.question: What is the empty weight center of gravity of an aircraft?

right.question: How should a mechanic determine rivet size, spacing, and edge distance when making a sheet-metal repair?
right.answer: When making a sheet-metal repair, a mechanic should determine rivet size, spacing, and edge distance by duplicating the original aircraft structure’s rivet size, spacing, and edge distance unless structural deficiencies are suspected. If structural deficiencies are suspected, the minimum edge distance and rivet spacing should be determined as follows: for single row rivets, the edge distance should not be less than 2 times the diameter of the rivet and spacing should not be less than 3 times the diameter of the rivet [1]. Additionally, rivet size, splicing, and rivet pattern must be exactly the same as the manufactured seams at the edges of the original sheet, and if the two manufactured seams are different, the stronger one will be copied [2]. The acceptable drill size for rivets may be found in MIL-HDBK-5 or MMPDS-10, and proper drill size must be used to avoid decreasing effective tensile areas in stressed members [4].

right.question: What practices does the circular recommend for repairing corrosion damage, and when should a damaged part be replaced?
right.answer: The circular recommends that repair of corrosion damage includes removal of all corrosion and corrosion products. If the corrosion damage is severe and exceeds the damage limits set by the aircraft or parts manufacturer, the part must be replaced [1]. If manufacturer information and limits are not available, a DER must be consulted before the aircraft or part is returned to service [1].

right.question: How does the circular describe selecting and installing bolts, nuts, and safety devices?
right.answer:
The circular describes selecting and installing bolts, nuts, and safety devices as follows:

- Bolts and nuts must be locked or safetyed, except self-locking nuts [2].
- For bolt holes, especially in primary connecting elements, close tolerances apply; it is generally permissible to use the first-lettered drill size larger than the nominal bolt diameter, except when AN hexagon bolts are used in light-drive fit (reamed) applications [2].
- Safety devices such as safety wire, cotter pins, and self-locking nuts are used to prevent loosening due to vibration [3].
- For safety wiring, when using the double-twist method, a minimum wire diameter of .032 inch should be used on parts with a hole diameter larger than .045 inch; .020-inch wire is specified for smaller holes [4].
- Cotter pins should be selected to be the largest size that fits the cotter pin hole and/or nut slots, and should not be reused [5].
- Cotter pins should be installed with the end rolled and tucked to prevent injury, and the prong must be firmly seated against the bolt shank or nut without exceeding bolt diameter or contacting the washer surface [5].

These instructions provide specific guidance on selection and installation of bolts, nuts, and safety devices in accordance with the aircraft maintenance standards.

right.question: What procedures does it describe for inspecting, preserving, or repairing fabric-covered aircraft surfaces?
right.answer:
The procedures for inspecting, preserving, or repairing fabric-covered aircraft surfaces include:

- All materials used for repairs must be of a quality at least equal to the original materials, and workmanship and repair methods must return the fabric covering to its original airworthy condition [1].  
- For repairs, any combination of hand-sewn seams and overlapped, doped fabric may be used [1].  
- Before installing a new fabric section or finishing tape, all pigmented dope coats (including aluminum-pigmented) must be removed to clear dope preliminary coats; this is done by applying appropriate dope thinner with a brush to soften the old dope, then scraping it down to the clear dope coats using a dull-bladed knife (sanding is optional) [1].  
- Dope must not run down the back side of the fabric or drip through the wing onto the opposite surface, as this causes cosmetic damage and shows as a high gloss finish [1].  
- When repairing fabric covering other than cotton or linen that was approved under a manufacturer’s type certificate (TC) or STC, the repair instructions must be followed as furnished by the aircraft manufacturer or STC-approved covering material supplier [3].  

These procedures cover inspection, preservation (via proper dope removal and application), and repair of fabric-covered surfaces. [1, 3]

right.question: What guidance does it give for inspecting and repairing aircraft electrical wiring and connections?
right.answer:
Guidance for inspecting and repairing aircraft electrical wiring and connections includes:

- Inspect equipment, electrical assemblies, and wiring installations for damage, general condition, and proper functioning to ensure continued satisfactory operation of the electrical system [1].
- Inspect wire annually for abrasions, defective insulation, condition of terminations, and potential corrosion [2].
- Grounding connections for power, distribution equipment, and electromagnetic shielding must be given particular attention to ensure electrical bonding resistance has not been significantly increased by loosening of connections or corrosion [2].
- Wires and cables should be visually inspected for adequacy of support, protection, and general condition throughout [4].
- Wires must be supported by suitable clamps, grommets, or other devices at intervals of not more than 24 inches, except when contained in troughs, ducts, or conduits [4].
- Metal stand-offs must be used to maintain clearance between wires and structure; tape or tubing is not acceptable as an alternative [4].
- Before performing any inspection or maintenance, turn off all electrical power for personal safety and to avoid the possibility of fire [4].
- Replace damaged or defective components with identical parts, aircraft manufacturer’s approved equipment, or equivalent in operating characteristics, mechanical strength, and environmental specifications [1].
- When using wire sizes smaller than #20, pay particular attention to mechanical strength and installation handling, such as vibration, flexing, and termination [2].
- For interconnecting airframe applications, #24 gauge wire must be made of high-strength alloy [2].
